planting.note: Propagate from stem-tip cuttings rooted in moist, warm (70-75F) potting mix or perlite; new plants need a season of steady humid warmth before they begin producing their showy calyces.

directions: Alloplectus calochlamys is a soft-wooded, hairy-leaved subshrub from the cloud forests of Colombia and Ecuador, grown not for its small hidden yellow corolla but for the inflated, bright orange-red calyx that encloses it, held in clusters at the stem tips and leaf axils nearly year-round in warm, humid conditions. Grow it in a loose, peat- or bark-based mix in a pot with excellent drainage, in bright but sunless shade such as an east window or a terrarium, since direct sun scorches the fuzzy foliage. Keep the mix evenly moist but never soggy, and provide high humidity (a terrarium, greenhouse, or pebble tray) to prevent leaf-edge browning. Pinch growing tips regularly to keep the naturally lanky stems bushy and well furnished with calyces.
sources: The Gesneriad Society — Alloplectus species profiles

planting.note: Establish rooted stem cuttings in a humusy, well-drained shade bed or large container; the shrub is slow to bulk up its first year but then grows steadily in warm, humid shade.

directions: Besleria lutea is a soft-stemmed, understory shrub of Neotropical forests from Mexico through the Caribbean and tropical South America, naturalized in shaded hammocks of South Florida, where its slender glossy leaves and small clusters of tubular yellow flowers are a familiar sight along forest edges. The flowers are followed by round, fleshy, orange-to-red berries that are a favored food of songbirds, and hummingbirds work the blooms. Plant it in humus-rich, moisture-retentive but well-drained soil in dappled or filtered shade, protected from direct midday sun and from frost, and prune lightly after flowering flushes to keep the lax stems from becoming leggy. It makes an effective informal flowering and fruiting understory shrub beneath larger shade trees in warm, frost-free gardens.
sources: Flora of the Caribbean — Gesneriaceae: Besleria
University of Florida IFAS Extension — exotic Gesneriaceae in South Florida hammocks

planting.note: Start from semi-hardwood stem cuttings or air-layers in a warm, humid propagation bed; young plants are coarse-leaved but slow, taking a year or more to reach flowering size.

directions: Rhytidophyllum tomentosum is a coarse, large-leaved Caribbean gesneriad shrub from the limestone forests of Hispaniola and Puerto Rico, bearing thick, felted, strongly wrinkled (rugose) leaves that give the genus its common 'woolly' character. Clusters of pale greenish-cream, tubular flowers are produced along the older wood and are pollinated by hummingbirds and, in its native range, by bats, with the blooms followed by fleshy berries. Grow it in dappled or filtered shade in deep, well-drained, humus-rich soil, sheltered from strong wind that can tatter the oversized leaves, and allow it room to develop its naturally open, small-tree-like habit over several seasons. Its bold tropical texture makes it a striking shade-garden specimen in frost-free climates or large conservatory plantings.
sources: Flora of the Greater Antilles — Gesneriaceae: Rhytidophyllum

planting.note: Root stem-tip cuttings in a warm, humid propagating mix; as a highland species it tolerates cooler nights than most tropical gesneriads but still needs frost protection.

directions: Moussonia deppeana is a softly velvety-leaved shrub from the cool, cloud-forest highlands of Mexico and Guatemala, closely related to Kohleria, with large heart-shaped leaves tinted red along the veins and undersides. Terminal clusters of bright red-orange, narrowly tubular flowers appear over a long season and are visited readily by hummingbirds. It prefers filtered or dappled shade with cooler, buoyant air rather than the hot, stagnant humidity suited to many lowland gesneriads, and benefits from a loose, humus-rich, well-drained mix kept evenly moist in the growing season and slightly drier in winter. Pinch young plants to encourage branching, since unpinched stems can become tall and sparse.
sources: The Gesneriad Society — Moussonia species profiles

planting.note: Root short stem cuttings in damp sphagnum or a loose, bark-based epiphyte mix; mount or pot in an open, fast-draining medium since the species grows naturally lodged in tree-bark crevices and rots in dense, wet soil.

directions: Codonanthe gracilis is a small, trailing epiphytic gesneriad from the lowland rainforests of Costa Rica, Panama, and Colombia, with slender wiry stems and small, somewhat fleshy, glossy leaves that make it well suited to hanging baskets and mounted epiphyte culture. Small white, tubular, bell-shaped flowers marked with purple spotting in the throat appear along the trailing stems and are followed by round, soft orange-to-red berries that persist attractively for weeks. Grow it in a loose, open, bark- or sphagnum-based mix that drains quickly, in bright shade with high humidity, and allow the surface to approach dryness between waterings to avoid root and stem rot. Its fine, cascading texture makes an excellent companion basket plant alongside bolder trailing gesneriads such as Columnea and Nematanthus.
sources: The Gesneriad Society — Codonanthe species profiles
Flora of Costa Rica — Gesneriaceae: Codonanthe

planting.note: Start scaly rhizomes in warm (70F+), humus-rich potting mix in spring as growth resumes after winter dormancy; divide congested rhizome clumps when repotting.

directions: Gloxinia perennis is the original rhizomatous South American species for which the whole 'gloxinia' group of gesneriads was named, native to humid forests from Trinidad and Venezuela to Peru. It produces somewhat gangly, softly hairy stems with large, heart-shaped, quilted leaves, and in late summer bears nodding, bell-shaped, violet-blue flowers with a paler, often spotted throat held in the upper leaf axils. Grow it in bright, filtered shade in a loose, well-drained, humus-rich mix, watering freely while in active growth and withholding water once the foliage yellows and dies back, allowing the scaly rhizome to rest dry and cool over winter before repotting and restarting it in spring. Its tall, informal habit suits it to the back of a shaded container grouping or a warm greenhouse bed rather than a tidy windowsill pot.
sources: The Gesneriad Society — Gloxinia perennis species profile
Flora of the Venezuelan Guayana — Gesneriaceae

planting.note: Divide scaly rhizomes or root stem cuttings in warm, humid conditions in spring; the plant bulks up quickly into a dense clump its first growing season.

directions: Chrysothemis pulchella is a rhizomatous gesneriad from the Caribbean and northern South America grown for its glossy, strongly quilted, ribbed foliage and its clusters of bright yellow flowers that emerge from showy, inflated, orange-red calyces at the stem tips. It spreads from scaly rhizomes into a dense, leafy clump and tolerates lower light and higher humidity than many flowering houseplants, making it a good choice for terrariums, bottle gardens, or humid shaded corners. Keep the mix consistently moist and warm, since the species dislikes both drying out and cold drafts, and provide bright, indirect light rather than direct sun to prevent leaf scorch. After flowering, the rhizomes can be left in the pot to produce a fresh flush of growth the following season.
sources: The Gesneriad Society — Chrysothemis species profiles
Flora Mesoamericana — Gesneriaceae: Chrysothemis
